lessons.hook: Set out cards of the Mass in a row. “What do you see at Mass?”
lessons.assess: Ask children to put four Mass cards in order.

script.open: Show the children a loaf of bread, and ask, “What happens at Mass? What do we do?” Let them name things. “We are going to put the parts of Mass in order, like pieces of a puzzle.”
teach: Say: “Mass is the greatest prayer of the Church. At Mass, Jesus is with us in a special way. The Mass has two big parts. In the first part, we listen to God’s word. In the second part, we share in Jesus’ gift, the Eucharist.”

Tell Luke 24:13-35 briefly: “After Jesus rose, two friends were walking to a town called Emmaus. They were sad. A stranger joined them, and he explained the Scriptures to them. When they got to the village, they asked him to stay for dinner. He took bread, blessed it, broke it and gave it to them. And suddenly they recognized him. It was Jesus! Then he disappeared. They said, ‘Did not our hearts burn within us while he spoke?’”

Say: “The Mass is just like this. First we listen to the readings, and the priest explains. Then the priest takes bread and wine and says Jesus’ words, and they become Jesus’ Body and Blood. We receive Jesus in Communion. And then we are sent out to tell people about him.”
ask: What are the two big parts of Mass? (Listening to God’s word, and the Eucharist.)
Who is with us at Mass? (Jesus.)
How did the two friends know it was Jesus? (When he broke the bread.)
practice: Prepare picture cards for the Mass: the entrance, the readings, the homily, the offering of bread and wine, Communion, and the blessing.
Mix the cards up, and have children put them in order.
For each, ask: “What do we do here?” and “What do we say?”
Practice the responses: “And with your spirit,” “Thanks be to God,” “Amen.”
script.close: Say the prayer together: “Lord, I am not worthy to receive you, but only say the word and I shall be healed.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “At Mass, listen for the Gospel.”

tryit: Put the Mass pictures in order.
Tell what happens in each one.
lessons.saintStory:
Justin was born about the year 100 in a town in the land of Samaria. He loved to study and was always looking for the truth. He tried many kinds of teachers, then one day he met an old man by the sea who told him about Jesus. Justin became a Christian.
He traveled to Rome and opened a school. He wrote a letter to the emperor to explain what Christians believed and what they did on Sunday. He described the very same things we do at Mass: readings from the Bible, a talk, prayers, bread and wine brought forward, and the people saying “Amen.”
Justin was put to death for his faith around the year 165. He is called Justin Martyr. He shows us that the Mass is very old, and that Christians have gathered like this since the beginning.

lessons.title: Being sorry and forgiven
lessons.idea: When we sin we can say sorry. In Reconciliation the priest, in Jesus’ name, forgives us.
lessons.question: Who forgives our sins?
lessons.activity: Practice an examination of conscience with simple questions and an Act of Contrition.
teach: Teach that God is always ready to forgive, and Reconciliation lets us say sorry and hear his forgiveness through the priest. The feeling to aim for is relief and trust, never dread.

CCC 1440: sin damages our friendship with God and the Church, and conversion brings forgiveness and reconciliation. CCC 1441: only God forgives sin; Jesus gives that power. CCC 1449: the priest absolves in the name of the Father, Son and Spirit.

Say: “When we do wrong we tell God we are sorry, and he is glad to forgive, like the shepherd who finds his lost sheep. In Reconciliation the priest speaks for Jesus.” To “Will the priest tell?”, say: “No, never; it is a secret.”

Never use the sacrament as a threat or punishment, and watch for scrupulous or anxious children. Do not expect lists of sins; a few simple ones suffice. Some children’s “sins” are accidents; teach the difference gently.
Ask: “What does God do when we say sorry?” Listen for forgives and is glad. Also ask what words we say; a child who offers “I am sorry” and “I will try again” has understood.
talk: How does God feel when we say sorry?
Who helps us say sorry?
How do we feel after?
quiz: In Reconciliation, the priest…|Judges|Hides|Scolds|Forgives in Jesus’s name|3|CCC 1461.
God’s forgiveness is…|Lost|Always ready|Late|Rare|1|CCC 1443.
We tell the priest our…|Sins|Games|Dreams|Toys|0|CCC 1456.
Why can the priest forgive our sins?|He has never sinned|He acts in Jesus’ name|He is the oldest in the parish|He is holier than we are|1|In Reconciliation the priest forgives in Jesus’ name.
After Confession, how can we feel?|Embarrassed forever|Forgiven and at peace|Free to sin again|Still afraid of being caught|1|God’s forgiveness brings peace.
lessons.life: Practice saying “I’m sorry, and I will try again.”
lessons.saint: John Vianney: he heard confessions for hours so people could meet God’s mercy.
misc: “God stops loving me when I sin.”
lessons.mem: O my God, I am sorry for my sins. Help me to do better. Amen.
lessons.hook: Tell the story of the lost sheep. “How does the shepherd feel when he finds it?”
lessons.assess: Ask: “What do we say when we are sorry?”

script.open: Spill a little bit of water on the floor and say, “Oops. I made a mess. What do I need to do?” Let them say to clean it up. “When we do something wrong, we make a kind of mess in our hearts. And God has a way to clean it up.”
teach: Tell Luke 15:1-10: “Jesus told a story about a shepherd with one hundred sheep. One got lost. What did the shepherd do? He left the other ninety-nine and went to find the lost one. When he found it, he put it on his shoulders and went home happy. And he said to his friends, ‘Come and celebrate with me.’ Jesus said that God is like that shepherd, and that there is joy in heaven over one person who says sorry.”

Say: “When we sin, we hurt God, other people and ourselves. But God is always ready to forgive. Jesus gave the Church a special sacrament so we can hear his forgiveness. It is called Reconciliation, or Confession. We tell our sins to the priest, he gives us advice, and then, in Jesus’ name, he says, ‘I absolve you from your sins.’”
Say: “It may feel scary. But it is a wonderful gift. We get to hear God say, ‘I forgive you.’ We start fresh. We feel light and happy again.”
ask: Who is the shepherd in the story? (Jesus, or God.)
What does God want to do when we are sorry? (Forgive us.)
What do we do first when we get ready for Confession? (Think about what we did wrong.)
practice: Teach the first steps for a child: 1. Say a short prayer. 2. Think about the day: Did I obey? Was I kind? Did I tell the truth? 3. Say what I did wrong. 4. Say the Act of Contrition.
Practice thinking through three questions with the group, quietly.
Say the Act of Contrition line by line: “O my God, I am sorry for my sins. Help me to do better. Amen.”
Close with a “Thank you, God, for forgiving us.”
script.close: Pray the Act of Contrition together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Ask when you can go to Confession as a family.”

tryit: Listen to the story of the lost sheep.
lessons.saintStory:
John Vianney was born in France in 1786. He was a farm boy who found it very hard to study, but he wanted to be a priest more than anything. After years of effort, he was ordained, and in 1818 he was sent to a tiny village called Ars.
The village was poor and hardly anyone went to church. Father Vianney visited the people, taught the children and prayed. Slowly, hearts changed. People began to come to him to confess their sins, so many that he spent up to sixteen hours a day in the confessional, and people traveled from far away to see him. He ate little and slept very little.
He is called the Curé of Ars, and is the patron of parish priests. He shows us that God’s mercy is great, and that a priest in Confession is a way for us to meet it.

units.title: Living as Jesus’ friends
units.eq: How do friends of Jesus live?

lessons.title: The Golden Rule
lessons.idea: Treat others as you want to be treated. This is how Jesus teaches us to love.
lessons.question: How do you want others to treat you?
lessons.activity: Role-play kind and unkind responses; practice the kind ones.
teach: Get across that we love as Jesus teaches by treating others the way we want to be treated. At six this turns faith into small daily choices on the playground and at home.
CCC 1789 names the Golden Rule (Matthew 7:12) as a rule that applies in every case. CCC 2055: Jesus sums up the Law as love of God and neighbor. We do it because we love God, not only to be fair.

Say: “How do you want people to treat you? Do that to them.” To “What if they are mean to me?”, say: “We still try to be kind, and we tell a grown-up if we are hurt or unsafe. Being kind does not mean letting someone hurt you.”
Do not suggest children should stay quiet when bullied or hurt. Avoid reducing the rule to “be nice so they like you.” Notice children who are often left out and be careful role-playing unkindness.
Give a short scene (someone has no one to play with) and ask what a friend of Jesus does. Listen for specific actions. Later watch for the rule in play.
talk: How do you want to be treated?
What is a kind word?
How can you help someone who is left out?
quiz: The Golden Rule says…|Treat others as you want to be treated|Win|Hide|Be first|0|Matthew 7:12.
Jesus taught us to…|Fight|Hide|Love|Buy|2|John 13:34.
A kind act is…|Yelling|Taking|Sharing|Pushing|2|Luke 6:31.

Anna’s friend is sad. What would the Golden Rule say?|Wait for her to come and ask|Be kind to her as you would want|Tell her loudly to cheer up|Leave her all alone to think|1|Treat others as you want to be treated.
Why is a small kind act important?|It makes us look good to others|It gets us a reward later|It makes the school day end sooner|It shows Jesus’ love|3|Kind acts show Jesus’ love.
lessons.life: Be the first to include a classmate who is alone.
lessons.saint: Elizabeth of Hungary: a queen who fed the poor.
lessons.mem: Do to others what you would have them do to you. (Matthew 7:12)
lessons.hook: Act out sharing a toy two ways. “Which way would you like?”
lessons.assess: Ask for an example of the Golden Rule.

script.open: Play “the unfair snack”: give one child a cookie and tell the others they cannot have any. Ask, “How did that feel? What if I did that to you?” Then say, “Jesus gave us a simple rule to help us in these moments.”
teach: Say: “Jesus said, ‘Do to others whatever you would have them do to you.’ (Matthew 7:12) We call this the Golden Rule. It is golden because it is so valuable. It means: before you do or say something, ask yourself, ‘How would I feel if someone did this to me?’”

Say: “If you would like someone to share, then you share. If you would like to be invited, then you invite someone. If you do not like being called names, do not call anyone names. If you want to be forgiven, forgive.”

Say: “This is how Jesus teaches us to love. Loving someone means thinking about what they need and feel. The Golden Rule works at home, at school, at the playground, with friends and with people we do not like very much.”
ask: What is the Golden Rule? (Treat others how you want to be treated.)
What would you want if you fell down at the playground? (Help, kindness.)
Who can you treat with the Golden Rule this week? (Take answers.)
practice: Give two cards to pairs: “Kind way” and “Unkind way.” Read a situation (someone is alone at recess, someone spills their lunch).
Let one child act out an unkind response, and then a kind one.
Talk about how each one feels.
Say the Golden Rule together, three times, with a motion: point to self, then to others.
script.close: Pray: “Jesus, help us treat others the way we want to be treated.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Do one kind thing and tell us about it.”

tryit: Act out kind and unkind ways to treat someone.
lessons.saintStory:
Elizabeth was born in 1207, the daughter of the king of Hungary. When she was fourteen she married a good young man named Louis, who ruled a part of Germany. They loved each other and loved God.
Elizabeth could have lived in a castle with all kinds of fine food and clothes, but she paid attention to the poor. She gave away food and money. She built a hospital and cared for the sick herself. Once, the story goes, she was carrying bread to the poor under her cloak and when someone asked what she had, it had turned into roses.
Elizabeth’s husband died when she was twenty. She gave up her riches to serve the poor, and she died at twenty-four. She shows us how to treat others as we want to be treated: with kindness.

lessons.title: Obey and honor
lessons.idea: We honor our parents and teachers. We follow rules that keep us safe and help us grow.
lessons.question: Who helps keep you safe?
lessons.activity: Make a thank-you card to a parent or teacher.
teach: The aim: honoring parents and teachers means listening and respecting them because they care for us, as Jesus did at Nazareth. At six this is about trust and safety, not blind fear.

CCC 2214: the honor owed to parents is rooted in God’s fatherhood. CCC 2216: respect shows in docility and obedience. This is the fourth commandment, which promises blessing and belongs with love of God.

Say: “Grown-ups help us stay safe and learn, so we listen and say thank you. Jesus obeyed Mary and Joseph.” To “What if they ask something wrong?”, say: “God comes first; tell another grown-up you trust.”

Family situations vary: some children live with an unsafe or absent parent or with foster carers. Say “the grown-ups who care for you.” Never suggest obeying anyone who hurts them; teach telling a safe adult.
Ask: “Who takes care of you, and how can you show respect?” Listen for concrete ways like listening, helping, thanking. Praise honest answers about finding it hard.
talk: Who keeps you safe?
Why are rules good?
How do you honor your parents?
quiz: The fourth commandment says…|Rest|Don’t lie|Don’t steal|Honor your father and mother|3|Exodus 20:12.
Jesus obeyed…|Nobody|Strangers|Soldiers|Mary and Joseph|3|Luke 2:51.
Obeying helps us…|Grow|Hurt|Fight|Hide|0|CCC 2216.
Why do we follow rules at home and school?|They make our days harder|They prove who is the boss|They keep us safe and help us grow|They keep adults happy with us|2|Rules help us grow and show honor.
Jose is asked to clean his room. What is the best response?|Do it only if he is paid|Say he will do it later|Do it cheerfully|Pretend that he did not hear|2|Obeying shows we honor our parents.
lessons.life: Say “Yes, Mom/Dad” cheerfully this week.
lessons.saint: Dominic Savio: a boy saint who obeyed his teacher and did small things with great love.
lessons.mem: Honor your father and mother.
lessons.hook: Show thank-you cards. “Who takes care of you? How can you thank them?”
lessons.assess: Ask: “How can you honor your family?”

script.open: Say, “I need two volunteers: one to be a ‘parent’ and one to be a ‘child.’ The parent says, ‘Please put your shoes away.’ The child can do three things: ignore, argue or obey. Which is best, and why?” Let them act it out and talk about it.
teach: Say: “One of God’s commandments says, ‘Honor your father and your mother.’ This is the fourth commandment, and the first one with a promise: ‘so that you may live long.’ (Ephesians 6:1-3) To honor means to respect and love, and to listen.”

Say: “Our parents, teachers and others take care of us. They give us food, a home, help and love. They make rules to keep us safe and to help us grow. When we obey them, we show love, and we help our family be happy. Remember that Jesus obeyed Mary and Joseph.”

Say: “It is not always easy! Sometimes we want to do something else. But when we obey with a good heart, we are growing in goodness. We can also say thank you. A thank-you is a way of honoring someone.”
ask: Why do we obey our parents and teachers? (To honor them, and because they love and take care of us.)
How did Jesus treat Mary and Joseph? (He obeyed them.)
How can you say thank you to your parents? (Words, help, a card, a hug.)
practice: Give each child a folded piece of paper and crayons.
Say: “Decorate the front of your card. Inside, we will write why we are thankful.”
Help each child write “Thank you for ______” and sign their name.
Let them decorate with stickers or drawings, then take the cards home.
script.close: Pray: “God, bless our parents and teachers.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Give the card, and give a hug.”

tryit: Give it to your parent or teacher.
lessons.saintStory:
Dominic Savio was born in Italy in 1842 to a poor family. He was a quiet, cheerful boy who loved to pray. At seven he made his First Communion, and he made some promises to God. One of them was: “I will rather die than sin.”
When Dominic was twelve, he went to a school in Turin run by Saint John Bosco, a priest who taught boys who had no one to look after them. Dominic obeyed his teachers, helped younger boys with their studies, and stopped fights. He said that holiness is being very cheerful and doing small things with great love.
Dominic died when he was only fourteen. He shows us that children can be saints, and that listening to parents and teachers is one way we love God.

lessons.title: Caring for creation and for the poor
lessons.idea: We take care of the world and share with people in need. Jesus cares for the poor.
lessons.question: What can we share?
lessons.activity: Collect canned goods or toys. Plant a small plant.
teach: Teach two linked ideas: the world is God’s gift to look after, and Jesus asks us to share with the poor. Children can do real, small acts of care and sharing.

CCC 2415: the seventh commandment calls for respect for creation. CCC 2443: God blesses those who help the poor, and Matthew 25 shows that what we do for the least we do for Christ. Genesis 2:15 gives humans the garden to tend.

Say: “God lets us look after his world, so we don’t waste or litter, and we share what we have with people in need, because Jesus is in them.” To “Why are people poor?”, say: “Sometimes things are unfair, and God asks us all to help.”

Some children in the class may be the ones in need, so avoid “poor people” as a distant group; speak of “families who need help.” Do not shame what children have. Give a task they can complete and keep it dignified.
Choose one action (collect for a food bank, tidy the yard, plant a seed) and ask who it helps and why. Listen for “Jesus is in the people we help” or “God gave us the world.”
talk: How can we care for the earth?
Who needs our help?
What can you share?
quiz: God asked humans to…|Ignore it|Sell it|Destroy it|Care for creation|3|Genesis 2:15.
Jesus cares for…|Nobody|Only the rich|The poor|Kings|2|Matthew 25.
Sharing is…|Boring|Silly|A way to love|Wrong|2|CCC 2447.

You find trash at the park. What shows care for God’s world?|Kick it into the bushes quickly|Leave it for someone else to find|Pick it up and put it in the bin|Tell others that it is not yours|2|God asked humans to care for creation.

Why should we help people who are poor?|Helping them will make us rich|It is a school rule to follow|Jesus says what we do for them we do for him|Only grown-ups are asked to help|2|What we do for the poor we do for Jesus.
lessons.life: Pick up trash at the park and share a snack.
lessons.saint: Martin of Tours: a soldier who shared his cloak with a poor man on a freezing night.
lessons.mem: Whatever you did for one of the least of these, you did for me. (Matthew 25:40)
lessons.hook: Hold a small plant. “God put us in the garden to take care of it.”
lessons.assess: Ask for one way to care for creation and one to help someone in need.

script.open: Say, “It is a freezing cold day. I have a nice warm coat, and someone else has none. What should I do?” Put your coat around a child, and let the children talk about what is fair and what is kind.
teach: Say: “God made the world and gave it to us. The garden of Eden was a place to care for. The Bible says God put people in the garden ‘to till it and keep it.’ (Genesis 2:15) We are God’s helpers. We take care of the earth, the plants, the animals, the water and the air.”

Say: “Jesus also cares about people who are poor, hungry or lonely. He told a story: ‘I was hungry, and you gave me food. I was thirsty, and you gave me drink. I was a stranger, and you welcomed me.’ Then he said, ‘Whatever you did for one of the least of these, you did for me.’ (Matthew 25:35-40) When we help someone in need, we are helping Jesus.”
Say: “What can a first grader do? Pick up trash, save water, share toys, bring food for the food pantry, make a card for a lonely neighbor, pray. Small things help.”
ask: Why do we take care of the world? (God made it, and gave it to us.)
Who does Jesus say we help when we help the poor? (Jesus himself.)
What can you do to help? (Share, give, pick up litter, pray.)
practice: Collect canned goods or toys (send a note home ahead of time), or look at photos of food pantry donations.
Let children place each item into a box and say, “For Jesus.”
Plant a small seed or plant in a cup. Say, “We take care of God’s world.”
Water it and put it in a sunny place.
script.close: Pray: “Jesus, help us care for the world and for the poor.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Choose one thing to share with someone who needs it.”

tryit: Bring a can of food or a toy to share.
lessons.saintStory:
Martin was born around the year 316 and joined the Roman army as a young man. He was not yet baptized, but he already tried to be good.
One bitterly cold winter day, as he rode through the city gate of Amiens in France, a beggar was freezing, barely dressed. Martin had nothing to give but his own cloak. He drew his sword, cut his cloak in two, and gave half to the beggar. That night, the story goes, Martin dreamed of Jesus wearing the half cloak, saying, “Martin gave me this.”
Martin was baptized soon after and later became a monk and a bishop. He teaches what Jesus said: whatever we do for the poor, we do for him.

units.title: Praying and the Church year
units.eq: How do we pray all year?

lessons.title: Ways we pray
lessons.idea: We pray to praise God, to thank him, to ask for help and to say sorry. We can pray anywhere.
lessons.question: What do you want to tell God today?
lessons.activity: Make four prayer cards: Praise, Thanks, Please, Sorry. Pick one to pray.
teach: The point: prayer is talking and listening to God, a friend who loves us, and it comes in four main ways: praise, thanks, asking and sorry. Children can start straight away in their own words.

CCC 2626: blessing and adoration are a response to God’s gifts. CCC 2629–2630: petition is the most spontaneous form, and the Church’s prayer is buoyed by hope. CCC 2623: the Spirit teaches us to pray. Say these as simple prayer types.

Say: “Prayer is talking to God like a good friend: wow, thank you, please, and sorry.” To “Does God hear me?”, say: “Yes, always. Sometimes the answer is wait or no, because he knows what is best, but he listens.”

Avoid treating prayer as a way to get things, or promising that God will give whatever we ask. A child who prayed for a sick parent or pet who died may feel God did not listen; acknowledge it and say God is with them.
Let the children say one prayer of each type aloud or by gesture (hands up, hands together, open hands). Ask which type they prayed. Their own words show it landed.
talk: What do you want to thank God for?
What do you want to ask?
When do you say sorry?
quiz: A prayer of thanks says…|Thank you, God|Hello|I’m sorry|Please|0|CCC 2638.
A prayer of petition asks for…|Silence|Toys only|Help|Nothing|2|CCC 2629.
Praise says…|I’m tired|You are great, God|Give me|Go away|1|CCC 2639.

Ella thanks God for dinner. Max asks God to help his sick grandma. Which pair names these prayers?|Saying sorry and thanks|Asking for help and praise|Thanks and asking for help|Praise and saying sorry|2|We pray to praise, thank, ask and say sorry.

Which prayer says sorry to God?|“God, thank you for my family”|“God, you are great and wonderful”|“God, please help me with my test”|“God, I did wrong; please forgive me”|3|A prayer of sorrow asks for forgiveness.
lessons.life: Pray one of each kind of prayer this week.
lessons.saint: Monica: a mother who prayed for her son for many years, and God answered.
lessons.mem: Thank you, God.
lessons.hook: Hold four cards: Praise, Thanks, Please, Sorry. “These are ways to talk to God.”
lessons.assess: Ask children to choose one card and say a prayer.

script.open: Hold up four small cards: a heart, a gift, a hand, a tear. Say, “These are four ways to talk to God. Let’s see if we can guess what each one means.” Let children guess before you explain.
teach: Say: “Prayer is talking and listening to God. You can pray anywhere: at home, in the car, in church, in bed. You can pray with your own words or with words you have learned. Here are four things we do when we pray.”

Say: “One: we praise God. Praise means telling God how wonderful he is. ‘God, you are great! You made the whole world.’ (Psalm 100.) Two: we thank God. ‘Thank you for my family. Thank you for food.’ Three: we ask God. ‘Please help my friend who is sick.’ Our asking is called a petition. Four: we say sorry. ‘God, I am sorry for what I did.’”

Say: “St. Paul said, ‘Do not worry about anything, but in everything, by prayer, with thanksgiving, make your requests known to God.’ (Philippians 4:6) We can tell God anything. He is our Father, and he loves to hear us.”
ask: What are four kinds of prayer? (Praise, thanks, please, sorry.)
When can you pray? (Any time, anywhere.)
What would you like to praise God for? (Take several.)
practice: Give each child four small cards: Praise, Thanks, Please, Sorry. Have them draw a symbol on each (a star, a gift, hands, a tear).
Mix them up, and let each child pick one card.
Ask the child to pray in their own words for that kind of prayer.
Everyone says “Amen” together after each prayer.
script.close: Say a short prayer of thanks together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Use the cards to pray with your family tonight.”

tryit: Choose a prayer card: Praise, Thanks, Please or Sorry.
lessons.saintStory:
Monica was born in North Africa around the year 331. She was a Christian and married a man who was not. Her son Augustine grew up clever, but he lived a wild life and did not follow Jesus.
Monica prayed for Augustine every day, for many years. She cried and begged God to help him. She even followed him across the sea to Italy. A wise bishop told her, “It is not possible that the son of so many tears should be lost.” She kept on praying.
After about seventeen years, Augustine did turn to God, and was baptized. He became a bishop and one of the greatest saints. Monica died soon after. She teaches us to pray and never give up, because God hears us.

lessons.title: Our Father and Hail Mary
lessons.idea: Jesus gave us the Our Father. Mary prays with us when we say the Hail Mary.
lessons.question: Which prayer do you like best?
lessons.activity: Pray the Our Father and a decade of the Rosary slowly together.
teach: The aim: the Our Father is the prayer Jesus himself gave, and the Hail Mary is how we pray with Mary. Children should learn the words and know that they are talking to our loving Father.
CCC 2759: the Lord gave his disciples the Our Father in answer to their request. CCC 2676: the Hail Mary joins the angel Gabriel’s greeting and Elizabeth’s words with a request for Mary’s prayers.

Say: “Jesus taught us to say ‘Our Father,’ which means God is our dad. In the Hail Mary we ask Mary to pray for us.” To “Why do we say ‘hallowed’?”, say: “It means holy, so we say God’s name is very special.”

Children who lost a father or have a difficult one may struggle with Father; stress that God is a perfect, loving Father. Avoid rote speed; check that words like trespass or womb are explained or skipped.
Pray the Our Father slowly with actions, then ask a child to explain one line in their words. Invite children to say the first half of the Hail Mary alone or in pairs.
talk: Which prayer is your favorite?
What do you ask in the Our Father?
Why do we pray the Hail Mary?
quiz: Jesus taught us…|The Hail Mary|The Gloria|The Creed|The Our Father|3|Matthew 6:9.
The Hail Mary is a prayer to…|Angels|Mary|Joseph|Peter|1|Luke 1:28.
The Rosary has…|Candles|Books|Beads|Stones|2|CCC 2678.
When we say the Hail Mary, what is happening?|Mary prays with us|Mary is too far away to hear|Mary is busy with other prayers|Mary answers us out loud|0|Mary prays with us when we say the Hail Mary.
Where does the Our Father come from?|Jesus taught it|Kings and queens made it|The saints wrote it long ago|A priest invented it|0|Jesus gave us the Our Father.
lessons.life: Pray a decade of the Rosary with your family.
lessons.saint: Dominic: tradition says Mary gave him the Rosary.
lessons.mem: Hail Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with thee; blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb, Jesus.
lessons.hook: Say, “Jesus taught his friends how to pray.”
lessons.assess: Ask children to pray the Our Father with you.

script.open: Show a string of rosary beads. Ask, “Has anyone seen these? What are they for?” Pass them around. “This is a special way to pray. But first, we will learn the two most important prayers.”
teach: Say: “The friends of Jesus said, ‘Lord, teach us to pray.’ And Jesus gave them the Our Father. It is the prayer of all God’s children. We pray it at Mass, at home, at school and in bed. It starts: ‘Our Father, who art in heaven’ because we are talking to God as our Father.”

Go through it in simple words: “We say his name is holy. We ask for his kingdom to come. We ask for our daily bread. We ask him to forgive us as we forgive others. We ask him to keep us safe from evil.”

Say: “The Hail Mary is the prayer we say to Mary. It starts with the angel’s greeting. When we say it, Mary prays with us. The Rosary is a prayer made of Our Fathers and Hail Marys. We use beads to count. One group of ten Hail Marys is called a decade. While we say them, we think about Jesus’ life.”
ask: Who gave us the Our Father? (Jesus.)
Who do we pray to in the Hail Mary? (Mary.)
What do the beads help us do? (Count the prayers while we think about Jesus.)
practice: Pass out a bead each (or pass around a rosary), and stand in a circle.
Pray the Our Father slowly, all together.
Pray one decade of Hail Marys together, using a rosary or counting on fingers. One child leads the first half, and the class answers the second half.
Say the Glory Be at the end.
script.close: Say the Glory Be together. Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Pray an Our Father and a Hail Mary with your family tonight.”

tryit: Pray a decade of the Rosary.
Listen to Mary praying with you.
lessons.saintStory:
Dominic Guzmán was born in Spain in about 1170. As a young man, he sold his books to feed the poor during a famine. He became a priest and spent many years traveling and preaching to people who had stopped believing in Jesus.
Dominic started a new order, the Dominicans, whose friars taught the faith to everyone. He loved to study, and he loved to pray. An old tradition says that Mary appeared to Dominic and gave him the Rosary, a way to pray with her and think about the life of Jesus, to help people who struggled to believe.
Whether that is how it started, the Rosary became a favorite prayer of the Church. Dominic shows us that praying slowly, with Mary, helps us know Jesus.

lessons.title: Advent, Christmas, Lent and Easter
lessons.idea: The Church year helps us remember Jesus. Each season has colors and signs.
lessons.question: What color do we see in Advent? In Easter?
lessons.activity: Color a church-year wheel with purple, white, green and red.
teach: Get across that the Church year helps us live Jesus’ story through the year, and each season has its own color and sign. Children love signs and pattern, and the year gives faith a rhythm.

CCC 1163: the Church celebrates Christ’s work through the year, beginning with Sunday. CCC 1168–1169: Easter is the source and the Feast of feasts, with the whole liturgical year around it. Colors follow tradition.

Say: “Advent we wait, Christmas we celebrate Jesus’ birth, Lent we prepare, and Easter we celebrate that he is alive.” To “Why is Lent sad?”, say: “It is not sad, it is a time to get ready, pray and share so Easter joy is bigger.”

Lent and Advent can become sweet-giving or rules for some families, and Christmas can be hard for children without a home or family. Avoid making seasons only about gifts or sacrifices. Note different customs at home.
Show four seasonal signs and ask children to match each with its season. Ask which season we are in now. Listen for the right sign and for Jesus, not only gifts or eggs.
talk: What color is Advent?
Why is Easter white?
What season are we in?
quiz: Advent is…|Red|Black|Purple|Orange|2|Liturgy.
Easter is…|Green|White|Black|Purple|1|Liturgy.
Ordinary Time is…|Green|Pink|Red|Blue|0|Liturgy.
A church has a wreath with purple candles. Which season is it?|Easter|Pentecost|Ordinary Time|Advent|3|Purple and the wreath are signs of Advent.

Why do the seasons of the Church have different colors?|They are only there for decoration|They help us remember Jesus’ story|They match the weather outside|They show who is in charge|1|Each season has colors and signs.
lessons.life: Look for the color of the season on the priest’s vestments.
lessons.saint: Isidore the Farmer: a field worker who prayed through the seasons of the year.
lessons.mem: Jesus is with us all year.
lessons.hook: Show four colors: purple, white, green, red. “Each means something.”
lessons.assess: Ask children to match colors and seasons.

script.open: Bring four items: a purple cloth, a white cloth, a green cloth and a red cloth. Hold them up one by one and ask, “Have you ever seen these colors at church? When?” Let the children share what they notice.
teach: Say: “The Church has a calendar, too. It is called the liturgical year, and it helps us remember the story of Jesus, season by season. Each season has a color.”

Say: “Purple is for Advent and Lent. These are times to get ready. In Advent we get ready for Christmas, and in Lent we get ready for Easter. White (or gold) is for Christmas and Easter, the happiest times. Green is for Ordinary Time, when we grow. Red is for the Holy Spirit, and for martyrs, who gave their lives for Jesus.”

Say: “Through the whole year, we can remember that Jesus is with us. The colors and signs, like the Advent wreath, the Christmas crib, ashes, the palms and the Easter candle, are like pictures to help us remember.”
ask: What color is used for Advent and Lent? (Purple.)
What color is used at Christmas and Easter? (White or gold.)
What does green mean? (Growing, Ordinary Time.)
practice: Give each child a circle divided into four or five pie pieces. Label them: Advent, Christmas, Lent, Easter, Ordinary Time.
Help children color each part: purple, white, purple, white, green.
Have children say a sentence about each season: “In Advent, we wait. At Christmas, Jesus is born.”
Hang the wheels up to look at throughout the year.
script.close: Pray: “Jesus, be with us all year.” Sign of the Cross. Send home: “Look at the color the priest wears this Sunday.”

tryit: Use purple, white, green and red.
lessons.saintStory:
Isidore was born in Madrid, Spain, around the year 1070. His family was poor, and he grew up to be a farmworker, plowing, sowing and harvesting for a wealthy landowner.
Isidore went to Mass every morning before work, and he prayed as he worked in the fields. The other workers complained that he was late, but the landowner saw that Isidore’s work always got done. Legend says that angels plowed for him while he prayed. He and his wife, María, were generous, and they shared their food with the poor, even when they had little.
Isidore is the patron of farmers. He teaches us that each season, in the fields and in the church year, is a time to pray, work and thank God.

units.title: Brave and kind
units.eq: How do I tell the truth, be kind to everyone, and take care of God’s gifts?

lessons.title: Telling the truth
lessons.idea: Six-year-olds lie to avoid trouble and to escape embarrassment. They need to hear that the truth is safe to tell and that God and the people who love them are glad when they do. The lesson uses the eighth commandment, conscience and the story of Juan Diego, who told the truth to a bishop.
lessons.question: Why is it hard to tell the truth sometimes?
lessons.activity: Play “Truth or tall tale.” Say two sentences about your day: one true, one made up. The class guesses which is true. Then practise saying a hard truth: “I broke it. I am sorry.” Clap for every brave truth.
teach: The goal is that telling the truth feels safe because God and the people who love them are glad. At six lies are about fear of trouble or embarrassment, so show that truth is less scary than hiding.

CCC 2464: the eighth commandment forbids misrepresenting the truth, because God is truth. CCC 2482: a lie is speaking a falsehood with the intent to deceive. CCC 1776: conscience is the voice in our heart calling us to do good.

Say: “Your conscience is a little voice in your heart that says ‘tell the truth.’ If you did something wrong, say it, say sorry, and fix it.” To “What if I get in trouble?”, say: “You may, but God and we are proud that you were honest, and it feels lighter.”

Do not punish honesty; if a child admits something, thank them first. Do not call a child a liar. Pretend play, imagination and mistakes are not lies. Safe grown-ups matter: some children fear harsh reactions at home.
Ask: “What can you say when you did something wrong?” Listen for “I did it, I am sorry.” Later, notice and praise a truthful moment with a specific comment.
talk: How does your tummy feel when you tell a lie?
How does it feel when you tell the truth?
What can you say if you break something?
quiz: What is a lie?|A secret|A joke|Saying something we know is not true to fool someone|A funny story|2|CCC 2482.
What did Jesus say about the truth?|It makes us free|It is scary|It is only for adults|It is boring|0|John 8:32.

lessons.hook: Tell a silly tall tale (“A giant elephant sat on my car this morning!”). Ask: “Is that true? How do you know?” Then say, “Today we learn why telling the truth is a brave and happy thing.”

script.open: Tell a silly tall tale: “An elephant sat on my car this morning!” Ask, “Is that true? How do you know?” Laugh with them. Then say, “It is fun to tell make-believe stories. But when something really happened, we tell the truth.”
teach: Say: “God is truth, and he wants us to tell the truth too. A lie is when we say something we know isn’t true to fool someone. The eighth commandment says we should not do that. When we tell the truth, people can trust us, and that makes us feel safe and happy.”

Say: “Telling the truth can be scary. Maybe you broke a cup, or didn’t finish your homework. You worry about getting in trouble. But Jesus said the truth makes us free. When you tell the truth, your heart feels light, like putting down a heavy backpack.”

Say: “If you told a lie, you can fix it. Say, ‘I did it. I am sorry.’ Then try to make it better. God forgives us, and so do the people who love us. Telling the truth is brave. We are going to practise being brave.”
ask: How does your tummy feel when you tell a lie?
How does it feel when you tell the truth?
What can you say if you break something?
practice: Play “Truth or tall tale”: say two sentences, one true and one made up. The class guesses.
Practise saying a hard truth together: “I broke it. I am sorry.”
Clap softly for every brave truth.
script.close: Make the Sign of the Cross together. Say, “God, help us to tell the truth. Amen.”

lessons.saintStory:
Juan Diego was a farmer who lived in Mexico about five hundred years ago. He was a kind, quiet man who walked a long way to Mass each Sunday. One cold morning in December 1531, he was on his way to church when he saw a beautiful lady on a hill. She said she was Mary, the mother of Jesus, and she asked him to tell the bishop to build a church on that spot.
Juan Diego went to the bishop and told him exactly what he had seen. The bishop did not believe him at first, and asked for a sign. Mary told Juan Diego to gather roses from the hill, though it was winter and there were no flowers. He found roses, and wrapped them in his cloak, called a tilma.
When he opened the cloak in front of the bishop, the roses fell out, and a picture of Mary appeared on the cloth. The bishop believed him. That cloak is still in Mexico City today. Juan Diego was honest and brave, and he was canonized in 2002.

lessons.title: Kind to everyone, even the one left out
lessons.idea: Six- and seven-year-olds know the sting of being left out and the thrill of being in a group. The Church’s teaching that every person has dignity, and that love means noticing the one who is alone, can be taught through a small habit: look around, find the one who is alone, and invite them. The lesson is built on the Good Samaritan and Matthew 25.
lessons.question: Has anyone ever left you out? How did that feel?
lessons.activity: Play “Find a friend.” Children walk around to music. When the music stops, each child finds one person who is alone and says “Do you want to play?” Then draw a picture of a time when you made someone feel welcome.
teach: Teach one habit: look around, notice who is alone, and invite them in. Six-year-olds know the sting of being left out; making it an action gives them a way to love like Jesus.

CCC 1700: human dignity is rooted in being made in God’s image. CCC 1822: charity is love of God and neighbor for God’s sake. CCC 2447: works of mercy include comforting. Matthew 25:40 says what we do to the least we do to Jesus.

Say: “Everyone is made by God and is special. If someone is alone, you can say ‘Want to play?’ That is how we love Jesus.” To “What if my friends say no?”, say: “Try a small thing, like saying hi, and ask a teacher for help.”

Some children are the ones left out, so avoid language that shames them as a project. Do not push children to befriend someone unsafe; tell an adult about bullying. Friendships cannot be forced, but kindness can be asked.
Ask: “What can you do if someone is alone at recess?” Listen for a concrete invitation. Later ask if anyone invited someone and how they felt.
talk: How does it feel to be left out?
What can you say to someone who is alone?
What did the Samaritan do that the others did not?

lessons.life: This week, look for one child who is alone at recess or lunch. Say, “Do you want to play?” or “Come sit with us.” Tell a parent how it went.
lessons.saint: Martin de Porres: a gentle man who was kind to everyone, even those who were unkind to him.

script.open: Place an empty chair in the circle. Say, “This chair is for someone who doesn’t have anyone to sit with.” Ask, “Who might sit here? What could we say to them to make them feel welcome?”
teach: Say: “God loves every person, and every person is special. That’s what the Church calls dignity. Jesus said that when we are kind to someone who is lonely or hurt, we are being kind to him. So every time you include someone, you are being kind to Jesus.”

Say: “Jesus told a story. A man was hurt on the road. Two people saw him and walked by. Then a Samaritan, a stranger, stopped. He bandaged the man’s wounds and took him to an inn. Jesus said, ‘Go and do the same.’ That means: when we see someone who needs help, we stop.”

Say: “At school we can notice who is alone. We can say, ‘Do you want to play?’ or ‘Come and sit with us.’ That’s a way of loving. It makes the other person happy, and it makes us happy too. And if someone is being unkind, we tell a grown-up.”
ask: How does it feel to be left out?
What could you say to someone who is alone?
What could you do if you see someone being unkind?
practice: Play music while children walk around. When it stops, each child finds one person and says, “Do you want to play?”
Stop again. Each child says, “Come and sit with us.”
Draw a picture of a time you welcomed someone.
script.close: Make the Sign of the Cross together. Say, “Jesus, help us to be kind to everyone.”

lessons.saintStory:
Martin de Porres was born in 1579 in Lima, Peru. His father was a Spanish nobleman and his mother was a freed slave from Panama. Because of this, Martin was often treated badly. He grew up poor, and when he was a teenager he asked to join the Dominican friars. At first they only let him work as a helper.
Martin cleaned floors, washed clothes and looked after the sick. He took care of everyone who came to the door: rich and poor, Spanish and African and Native Peruvian. He gave food to the hungry and medicine to the sick. He even took care of stray animals, and it is said that a dog, a cat and a mouse once ate from the same dish at his feet.
People were so moved by his goodness that the Dominicans made him a full brother. He died in 1639, and was canonized in 1962. He is the patron of people who work for justice and for all who are treated unfairly.

lessons.title: God’s good world: taking care of my body and of creation
lessons.idea: Children love animals, plants and their own bodies. The Church’s teaching on creation, the dignity of the body and the care of the earth invites them to see these as gifts to enjoy and to care for. The lesson offers small habits (washing hands, resting, planting, not wasting) and gratitude.
lessons.question: What is your favourite thing that God made?
lessons.activity: Take a “gift walk.” Look carefully at five things God made (a leaf, a bug, a cloud, your hand, a friend). Then plant a seed or care for a class plant, and name one way you will take care of your body this week.
teach: The message: the world and our bodies are God’s good gifts, so we thank him by taking care of them. At six this means small habits and wonder, not worry about the planet.

CCC 339: each creature has its own goodness, and God saw that it was good. CCC 2415–2418: we respect creation and owe animals kindness, though they are not equal to people. CCC 2288: life and health are precious gifts to care for.

Say: “God made everything good, including you. We say thank you by caring for plants and animals, washing hands, resting and eating well.” To “Why do animals die?”, say: “All living things have a time, and God cares for them; we are gentle with them.”

Avoid heavy climate fear, body shame, or food moralizing; some children have illness, disability, or little choice about food or sleep. Keep it positive, and tell a grown-up when sick or hurt. Do not equate animals with people.
Ask for one way to care for the world and one for their body. Listen for specific choices and a thank-you to God. Check a child’s plant or hand washing the following week.
talk: What is your favourite thing God made?
What can you do to take care of animals or plants?
How can you take care of your body?

lessons.life: This week, do one thing to take care of creation (put litter in the bin, water a plant, be gentle with a pet), and one thing to take care of your body (wash hands, go to bed on time).
lessons.saint: Isidore the Farmer: a hard-working farmer who prayed while he worked, and cared for animals and the earth.
misc: “Taking care of nature is only for grown-ups.”
lessons.mem: “God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good.” (Genesis 1:31)
lessons.hook: Hold up a seed. Ask: “What do you think is inside?” Plant it in a cup of soil. Say, “God made everything, and he gave us a job: to take care of it.”
lessons.assess: Ask each child to name one thing they will do to care for creation and one for their body.

script.open: Hold up a seed. Ask, “What do you think is inside?” Plant it in a cup of soil with the class. Say, “God made everything. He gave us a job: to take care of it.”
teach: Say: “In the beginning, God made the world, and he said it was very good. The sun, the sea, animals, plants, and you! Everything he made shows a little bit of how good God is. God made you in a special way, too. You are fearfully and wonderfully made.”

Say: “God gave us a job: to take care of what he made. We take care of plants and animals. We don’t waste. We don’t hurt them. This is called stewardship. We can plant seeds, put litter in the bin, and be gentle with animals. When we do, we thank God.”

Say: “We also take care of our bodies, because they are gifts. We wash our hands, eat good food, sleep, play outside. When we’re sick or hurt, we tell a grown-up. Taking care of ourselves and the world is a way of saying thank you to God.”
ask: What is your favourite thing that God made?
What is one way you can take care of an animal or a plant?
What is one way you can take care of your body?
practice: Go on a gift walk: look closely at five things God made.
Water the seed together and say, “Thank you, God, for growing things.”
Each child says or draws one way to care for creation and one way to care for their body.
script.close: Pray the grace before meals together. Say, “Thank you, God, for this beautiful world.”

lessons.saintStory:
Isidore lived in Spain about nine hundred years ago, near the city of Madrid. He was a farmer who worked for a rich landowner. He plowed the fields, planted seeds and looked after the animals. He and his wife, Maria, were poor, but they were happy and kind. They shared whatever they had with others, even when they had little.
Isidore loved to pray. He would go to Mass each morning before he began his work. Some of the other farmers complained to the landowner that Isidore came late to the fields. But the landowner saw that Isidore’s work was done well, and sometimes he even said he saw angels helping him plow.
Isidore died in 1130. In 1622 he was named a saint, and today he is the patron of farmers. He shows us that work done with love and prayer is a way of thanking God. He is also remembered for his kindness to animals.
